records.change: "Lord" becomes "sir"
records.note: As at John 6:34, the Greek "kyrie" is ambiguous between polite address and a confession of Christ's lordship; the NIV takes it as the former here.

records.change: Drops "going through the midst of them, and so passed by"
records.note: This clause, echoing Luke 4:30, is widely regarded as a scribal harmonization absent from the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows. It removes a vivid but non-doctrinal detail of Jesus's escape.

records.change: "Son of God" becomes "Son of Man"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "the Son of Man" here, a title Jesus uses of himself elsewhere; the Byzantine/Textus Receptus text underlying the KJV reads "the Son of God" instead. The NIV follows the earlier reading.

records.change: "Lord" becomes "sir"
records.note: Again the ambiguous "kyrie"; the healed man has not yet recognized Jesus's identity in this exchange, so the NIV renders it as plain address rather than a title.

records.change: Drops "as I said unto you"
records.note: This closing clause, referring back to an earlier statement, is present in the Byzantine/Textus Receptus text but missing from the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows. No doctrine turns on it.

records.change: Drops "Simon's son" from Judas's description
records.note: Manuscripts vary on how fully Judas is identified here; some include "Simon's son" and others do not. The NIV follows the shorter form; it is a genealogical detail, not doctrine.

records.change: "Believe not" becomes "does not keep them"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "does not keep" (or guard) my words rather than "does not believe"; the NIV follows this reading, shifting the verse's language from faith to obedience, though both are taught elsewhere in John.

records.change: Drops "because I go to the Father"
records.note: This clause is present in the Byzantine/Textus Receptus text, likely repeated by scribes from verse 17, but absent from the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows. The same statement appears in the very next verse.

records.change: Drops closing "Amen"
records.note: As at the end of Luke, the closing "Amen" is a scribal addition found in the Byzantine/Textus Receptus tradition but not in the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows.

records.change: "Commandments" becomes "instructions"
records.note: A translation choice rather than a manuscript difference: the Greek word covers both authoritative command and general instruction, and the NIV opts for the softer sense for what the risen Christ told the apostles.

records.change: "Hell" becomes "the realm of the dead"
records.note: The Greek is "Hades," the abode of the dead generally, which the KJV renders "hell" as it often does; the NIV's "realm of the dead" avoids implying the place of final punishment (Gehenna). Both translate the same Greek word.

records.change: Drops "Christ"; shortens the oath about David's throne
records.note: The earliest manuscripts have a shorter text here, lacking "according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ"; the NIV follows them, so the promised heir to David's throne is left unnamed as "Christ" in this verse, though the identification is made elsewhere in the sermon.

records.change: "Hell" becomes "the realm of the dead"
records.note: As at Acts 2:27, the Greek is "Hades"; the NIV's rendering avoids the connotation of final punishment that "hell" carries in modern English. (The verse also renders "Christ" as "Messiah," the same word in Greek and Hebrew.)

records.change: "Added to the church" becomes "added to their number"
records.note: Manuscripts differ between "to the church" and the idiom "to the same" (their number) here; the NIV follows the latter. The sense - believers being added daily - is unchanged.

records.change: "His Son Jesus" becomes "his servant Jesus"
records.note: The Greek "pais" can mean either "son/child" or "servant"; the KJV takes the former, echoing divine sonship, while the NIV takes the latter, echoing Isaiah's suffering servant. Both are defensible renderings of the same word.

records.change: "His Son Jesus" becomes "his servant"
records.note: The same ambiguous Greek word ("pais") as Acts 3:13; the NIV again renders it "servant" rather than "Son," favoring the Isaianic servant motif over the sonship title.

records.change: "Lord, thou art God" becomes "Sovereign Lord"
records.note: The NIV compresses the address into a single title, "Sovereign Lord," rather than the KJV's separate "Lord, thou art God"; the prayer's acknowledgment of God as maker of heaven and earth follows either way.

records.change: Drops "of the Lord" from the angel's description
records.note: The Byzantine text and Textus Receptus read "an angel of the Lord"; the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows, read simply "an angel." The Lord's involvement in Moses' call at the burning bush is still plain from the rest of the account.

records.change: "the Lord your God" shortened to "God"
records.note: The Textus Receptus has "the Lord your God will raise up"; the NIV follows the shorter earliest-manuscript reading, "God will raise up." This prophecy of a coming prophet like Moses, read as messianic, is otherwise unchanged.

records.change: Omits "calling upon God" before "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit"
records.note: The Textus Receptus has Stephen "calling upon God, and saying, Lord Jesus..."; the earliest manuscripts, followed by the NIV, lack "God," leaving only "Lord Jesus." The KJV's wording makes explicit that Stephen prayed to Jesus as God; the NIV still shows him praying to Jesus, but without that label attached.

records.change: Verse omitted: the eunuch's confession "Jesus Christ is the Son of God"
records.note: This verse is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and is widely held to be a later addition reflecting an early baptismal creed; the NIV omits it and renumbers the chapter accordingly. The confession of Jesus as Son of God is affirmed many times elsewhere in Acts and the Gospels.

records.change: Omits "it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks"
records.note: This clause is a well-known Byzantine/Textus Receptus expansion, borrowed from Paul's retelling of his conversion at Acts 26:14, and is absent from the earliest manuscripts of chapter 9. No doctrine is at stake; the idiom about resisting God is still present at 26:14.

records.change: Omits Saul's question and the Lord's reply before the command
records.note: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do? And the Lord said unto him, Arise" is another Byzantine harmonization, borrowed from Acts 22:10, missing from the earliest manuscripts of chapter 9. The content is preserved at its original locations in chapters 22 and 26.

records.change: Omits "in the name of the Lord Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows, lack this phrase describing how Paul spoke; the Textus Receptus includes it. Paul's bold preaching in Jesus' name is still described two verses earlier, at 9:27.

records.change: Omits "he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do"
records.note: This clause is in the Textus Receptus but absent from the earliest manuscripts, likely copied in from the angel's near-identical words to Cornelius in verse 32. No doctrine is affected, and the same instruction is given there.

records.change: Drops "wild beasts" from the list of animals
records.note: The earliest manuscripts list only four-footed animals, reptiles and birds; the Textus Receptus adds "wild beasts" as a fourth category. The parallel account at 11:6, retelling this vision, keeps all four categories in both texts.

records.change: Drops "which were sent unto him from Cornelius"
records.note: The Textus Receptus identifies the men as sent by Cornelius; the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows, just say "the men." The detail is not lost to the reader, since Cornelius sent them earlier in the chapter.

records.change: Drops "fasting"; Cornelius is only "praying"
records.note: The Textus Receptus has Cornelius "fasting... and praying"; the earliest manuscripts lack the fasting clause, and the NIV follows them. Fasting as a devotional practice is well attested elsewhere in Acts and the Gospels.

records.change: "this day have I begotten thee" becomes "today I have become your father"
records.note: Both texts have the same Greek, quoting Psalm 2:7's "I have begotten you"; the NIV chooses a paraphrase that reframes eternal begetting as becoming a father, a different image for Christ's sonship. The verse is quoted in its fuller form at Hebrews 1:5 and 5:5.

records.change: Drops "Christ" from "the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ"
records.note: Some early manuscripts lack "Christ" here, and the NIV follows them, leaving "the grace of our Lord Jesus." The statement that salvation is by grace, through the Lord Jesus, is unchanged.

records.change: "Known unto God are all his works" becomes "things known from long ago"
records.note: This is one of the most disputed readings in Acts; the earliest manuscripts have a much shorter, less specific text than the Textus Receptus, and the NIV follows the shorter form. The KJV's explicit statement of God's foreknowledge of his works is not asserted as plainly in the NIV's wording.

records.change: Omits the disputed teaching: "Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law"
records.note: The Textus Receptus quotes the false teaching directly; the earliest manuscripts, followed by the NIV, describe it only as "troubling your minds by what they said," without naming it. The circumcision-and-law controversy is still the subject of the whole chapter and is stated plainly elsewhere in it, at 15:1 and 15:5.

records.change: Verse omitted: "it pleased Silas to abide there still"
records.note: This verse is absent from the best early manuscripts and is generally regarded as a scribal addition explaining how Silas came to be with Paul in the next chapter. No doctrine is involved.

records.change: Drops "Christ" from "the Lord Jesus Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "the Lord Jesus" without "Christ," and the NIV follows them. The promise of salvation by belief in the Lord Jesus, given to the Philippian jailer, is unchanged.

records.change: "of one blood" becomes "from one" man
records.note: The Textus Receptus reads "of one blood"; the earliest manuscripts, followed by the NIV, lack "blood" and read only "from one." Both readings teach the common origin of all nations, but the specific image of shared blood is absent from the NIV.

records.change: "pressed in the spirit" becomes "devoted himself...to preaching"
records.note: This is a genuine textual variant: the earliest manuscripts read "occupied with the word" (preaching), where the Textus Receptus has "pressed in the spirit." The change affects only the description of Paul's inner state, not any doctrine.

records.change: Omits Paul's vow to "keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem"
records.note: This clause about a feast obligation is in the Textus Receptus but absent from the earliest manuscripts, and the NIV follows the shorter text. No doctrine is affected; it is a detail of Paul's travel plans.

records.change: "Christ Jesus" becomes "Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read simply "Jesus" as the one John pointed to; the Textus Receptus has "Christ Jesus," and the NIV follows the shorter reading. The identification of Jesus as the one to believe in is unchanged.

records.change: "the word of the Lord Jesus" becomes "the word of the Lord"
records.note: The Textus Receptus names Jesus specifically here; the earliest manuscripts, followed by the NIV, read only "the Lord." The gospel being spread is still unmistakably about Jesus from the surrounding context.

records.change: Omits "in the spirit" from Paul's decision to go to Jerusalem
records.note: Both texts have the same Greek phrase; the NIV simply does not translate "in the spirit," which commentators debate as referring either to Paul's own resolve or the Holy Spirit's leading. Either way, the phrase itself is missing from the NIV's rendering.

records.change: Drops "Christ" from "our Lord Jesus Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "our Lord Jesus" without "Christ," and the NIV follows them. Paul's summary of his message here, repentance toward God and faith in the Lord Jesus, is unchanged.

records.change: "the kingdom of God" becomes "the kingdom"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows, lack "of God" here; the Textus Receptus includes it. The kingdom Paul preached is still God's kingdom by context, even without the explicit phrase.

records.change: Omits "the multitude must needs come together"
records.note: This clause, predicting that a crowd will gather, is in the Textus Receptus but absent from the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows. No doctrine is affected.

records.change: Omits the Pharisees' warning "let us not fight against God"
records.note: This clause is in the Textus Receptus but missing from the earliest manuscripts, and the NIV follows the shorter reading. It echoes Gamaliel's similar warning at Acts 5:39, which is untouched.

records.change: Omits "and would have judged according to our law"
records.note: This is part of a well-known longer reading spanning Acts 24:6-8 that is found in the Textus Receptus but absent from the earliest manuscripts; the NIV follows the shorter text, which continues at verse 8 without a gap in sense. No doctrine is affected.

records.change: Verse omitted: Lysias forcibly took Paul from his accusers
records.note: This verse is part of the same longer Byzantine reading omitted at 24:6, absent from the earliest manuscripts; the NIV follows the shorter text and renumbers accordingly. It is a narrative detail with no doctrine at stake.

records.change: Omits that the centurion delivered prisoners to the guard's captain
records.note: The clause is present in the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus but absent from the earliest manuscripts, which the NIV follows here; it is a narrative detail, not a doctrinal point.

records.change: Omits the verse: the Jews' departure and dispute
records.note: The verse is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is judged by most textual critics to be a later scribal addition; it records a narrative detail, not doctrine.

records.change: Omits "of Christ" from "the gospel of Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, P46) lack "of Christ" here, which the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus include; the gospel is identified as Christ's throughout Romans regardless.

records.change: "did not believe" becomes "were unfaithful"
records.note: The Greek word can mean either disbelief or unfaithfulness; the NIV's choice shifts the sense toward covenant faithfulness, though the underlying text is the same.

records.change: Omits "our Lord" from "Jesus Christ our Lord"
records.note: The shorter "Christ Jesus" is found in the earliest manuscripts; the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus have the fuller title. Christ's lordship is affirmed throughout Romans regardless.

records.change: Omits "who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit"
records.note: This clause is absent from the earliest manuscripts and is thought to be a scribal addition copied from verse 4; without it, freedom from condemnation reads as unconditional rather than tied to how one walks.

records.change: "word of God" becomes "word about Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "word of Christ" where the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus have "word of God"; either way the point is that faith comes through hearing the gospel message.

records.change: Omits "otherwise work is no more work"
records.note: This clause restates the verse's first half and is missing from the earliest manuscripts, likely a scribal expansion; the point that grace and works are mutually exclusive still stands.

records.change: "God is able to make him stand" becomes "the Lord"
records.note: Some early manuscripts read "Lord" rather than "God" here; both refer to the one upholding the believer, so the point is unaffected.

records.change: Omits "he that regardeth not the day...he doth not regard it"
records.note: This balancing clause about not observing a day is missing from the earliest manuscripts and is considered a scribal duplication; the teaching on Christian liberty over days is unaffected.

records.change: "judgment seat of Christ" becomes "God's judgment seat"
records.note: The Byzantine text and Textus Receptus read "of Christ" while the earliest manuscripts read "of God"; 2 Corinthians 5:10 elsewhere confirms believers stand before Christ's judgment seat.

records.change: "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "our Lord Christ"
records.note: Some early manuscripts omit "Jesus" here; the reference to Christ as Lord is unchanged.

records.change: Omits "Christ" and the closing "Amen"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "our Lord Jesus" without "Christ" and lack the final "Amen," which is widely regarded as a later liturgical addition.

records.change: Omits the verse: "grace of our Lord Jesus Christ...Amen"
records.note: Most textual critics regard this verse as a scribal duplicate of verse 20's blessing, absent from the earliest manuscripts; the same blessing is given a few verses earlier.

records.change: Omits the closing note naming Phoebe and Cenchrea
records.note: This is a scribal subscription found in the Byzantine tradition, not part of Paul's original letter; most translations drop such subscriptions as later additions.

records.change: Omits "Christ" (twice) from "our Lord Jesus Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read the shorter "our Lord Jesus" in both places in this verse; the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus have the fuller title.

records.change: "day of the Lord Jesus" becomes "day of the Lord"
records.note: Some early manuscripts lack "Jesus" here; the reference is still to Christ's day of judgment.

records.change: Omits "and in your spirit, which are God's"
records.note: This clause is absent from the earliest manuscripts and thought to be a later addition paralleling "in your body"; the call to honor God with the body remains.

records.change: Omits "fasting" from "fasting and prayer"
records.note: "Fasting" is present in the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus but absent from the earliest manuscripts, likely a later ascetic addition; the verse still calls the couple to devote the time to prayer.

records.change: "Jesus Christ our Lord" becomes "Jesus our Lord"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts lack "Christ" here; Paul's claim to have seen the risen Lord is unaffected.

records.change: Omits "of Christ" from "the gospel of Christ"
records.note: Some early witnesses lack "of Christ" in this phrase; the gospel Paul preaches free of charge is Christ's gospel either way.

records.change: Omits "for the earth is the Lord's, and the fulness thereof"
records.note: This quotation of Psalm 24:1 is absent from the earliest manuscripts and generally judged a scribal addition harmonizing with verse 26; the instruction about eating for conscience' sake stands without it.

records.change: Omits "Take, eat" and "broken" for you
records.note: P46, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus lack both; the Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus have them. The NIV's "my body, which is for you" no longer says it is broken.

records.change: Omits "unworthily"; "the Lord's body" becomes "the body of Christ"
records.note: "Unworthily" is present in the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus but missing from the earliest manuscripts; the warning about discerning the body at communion is preserved either way.

records.change: "commandments" (plural) becomes "command" (singular)
records.note: Manuscripts differ between the singular and plural here; either way Paul claims his instruction carries the Lord's authority.

records.change: "the Lord from heaven" becomes "of heaven"
records.note: "Lord" is present in the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus but absent from the earliest manuscripts (Vaticanus, Sinaiticus, P46); Christ's heavenly origin is still the point being made.

records.change: "the Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "the Lord"
records.note: The shorter title is found in the earliest manuscripts; the call to love the Lord and the transliterated "Maranatha" are retained.

records.change: "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "the Lord Jesus"
records.note: Some early manuscripts lack "Christ" and "our" here; the content of the blessing is unchanged.

records.change: Omits the closing note naming the letter's bearers
records.note: This is a scribal subscription from the Byzantine tradition, not part of Paul's original text; the NIV drops it as a later addition, as it does elsewhere.

records.change: Drops the repeated "salvation" in the verse's second half
records.note: The earliest manuscripts have a shorter, less repetitive form of this verse than the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus; salvation is still named as the outcome of the Corinthians' endurance.

records.change: "the face of Jesus Christ" becomes "the face of Christ"
records.note: Some early manuscripts lack "Jesus" in this phrase; God's glory is still said to be seen in the face of Christ.

records.change: "the dying of the Lord Jesus" becomes "the death of Jesus"
records.note: Some early manuscripts omit "Lord" at this first mention; Jesus is still named as the one whose death and life are carried in the body.

records.change: "by Jesus Christ" becomes "through Christ"
records.note: Some early witnesses read simply "Christ" rather than "Jesus Christ" here; the reconciliation described is unaffected.

records.change: "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "the Lord Jesus"
records.note: Some early manuscripts lack "Christ" and "our" here; the statement that God is the Father of the Lord Jesus is unaffected.

records.change: Omits closing "Amen" and the scribal subscription
records.note: The final "Amen" and the note naming Titus and Luke as bearers of the letter are absent from the earliest manuscripts; both are widely regarded as later liturgical or scribal additions.

records.change: Omits "among you" from the crucifixion scene
records.note: The Alexandrian text lacks "among you" (en hymin), found in the Byzantine tradition and Textus Receptus; the sense of the verse is unaffected.

records.change: Omits "in Christ" from the covenant's confirmation
records.note: The earliest manuscripts lack "in Christ" (eis Christon) after "confirmed before of God", present in the Byzantine text and Textus Receptus; the covenant's basis in God's own promise is unchanged either way.

records.change: Heirship comes "through God," not "through Christ"
records.note: Some early manuscripts read "an heir through God" rather than "an heir of God through Christ"; NIV follows the shorter reading. Christ's mediating role in adoption is still taught earlier in the same chapter (Galatians 4:4-5).

records.change: Omits "in Christ Jesus"
records.note: The opening phrase "in Christ Jesus" is missing from the earliest manuscripts and thought to be a scribal echo of Galatians 5:6; the point that only the new creation matters is unaffected.

records.change: "the Lord Jesus" becomes just "Jesus"
records.note: Some early manuscripts drop "Lord" before Jesus in this closing remark about Paul's scars; the title is used of him throughout the rest of the letter.

records.change: Omits "by Jesus Christ" as creation's agent
records.note: The clause "by Jesus Christ" is absent from the earliest manuscripts and thought to be a later addition; Christ's role in creation is still affirmed elsewhere, e.g. Colossians 1:16 and John 1:3.

records.change: Omits "of our Lord Jesus Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read simply "the Father" here, without the added title, likely harmonised from Ephesians 1:3; Christ's relationship to the Father is stated plainly elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: "fruit of the Spirit" becomes "fruit of the light"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "light" rather than "Spirit" here, fitting the surrounding image of walking as children of light; the fruit described (goodness, righteousness, truth) is identical either way.

records.change: "fear of God" becomes "reverence for Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "Christ" rather than "God" here; the change attributes the reverence owed in mutual submission specifically to Christ rather than to God the Father.

records.change: Omits "of his flesh, and of his bones"
records.note: This clause, echoing Genesis 2:23, is missing from the earliest manuscripts and thought to be a later gloss; the union of Christ and the church it illustrates is still stated in the rest of the verse.

records.change: Content of verses 16 and 17 are swapped
records.note: Manuscripts differ on whether the clause about preaching from envy or the one about preaching from love comes first; both statements appear in the passage either way, only reordered between this verse and the next.

records.change: "thought it not robbery" becomes not "used to his own advantage"
records.note: A translation choice for harpagmos, the Greek being the same. The KJV says equality with God was rightly his; the NIV says he did not exploit it. Both affirm he was God.

records.change: Omits "by the same rule, mind the same thing"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts lack this clause, thought to be a scribal addition echoing Galatians 6:16; the exhortation to press on toward the goal is retained.

records.change: "with you all" becomes "with your spirit"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "with your spirit" in this closing blessing rather than "with you all"; both are benedictions on the whole church, worded differently.

records.change: Omits "and the Lord Jesus Christ" as source of grace
records.note: The earliest manuscripts name only "God our Father" as the source of grace and peace here, without the added "and the Lord Jesus Christ", likely harmonised to Paul's other openings; Christ is named repeatedly later in the same letter.

records.change: Omits "through his blood"
records.note: The phrase is in the Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus but not in Sinaiticus, Vaticanus or most early witnesses; the NIV follows the latter. Redemption through Christ's blood is still stated in Ephesians 1:7.

records.change: "God, the Father, and Christ" becomes "God, namely Christ"
records.note: This is one of the most disputed readings in the New Testament, with over a dozen manuscript variants; NIV's wording identifies the mystery of God directly with Christ, where the Textus Receptus lists God, the Father, and Christ as if distinct terms.

records.change: Omits "on the children of disobedience"
records.note: The phrase, which also appears in Ephesians 5:6, is missing from the earliest manuscripts of Colossians and thought to be copied in from there; God's coming wrath is still stated, just without naming its object.

records.change: "as Christ forgave you" becomes "as the Lord forgave you"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "the Lord" rather than "Christ" here; the reference is the same person either way.

records.change: "the peace of God" becomes "the peace of Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "Christ" rather than "God" here; the change attributes the peace that is to rule in believers' hearts specifically to Christ rather than to God the Father.

records.change: "sing...to the Lord" becomes "sing...to God"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "God" rather than "Lord" as the object of this thanksgiving; elsewhere in Paul both terms describe worship offered through Christ.

records.change: Omits "from God our Father, and the Lord Jesus Christ"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts end the greeting at "grace and peace to you", without naming its source; the fuller wording found in Paul's other openings is thought to be an early expansion of this, his shortest greeting.

records.change: "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "our Lord Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Christ" from this title; the fuller title is used elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "our Lord Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Christ" from this title in Paul's prayer; the fuller title is used elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "our Lord Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Christ" from this title; the fuller title is used elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "our Lord Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Christ" from this title describing the gospel that is obeyed; the fuller title is used elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: First "our Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "our Lord Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Christ" from the first mention of the title in this verse, though the fuller title is kept later in the same verse.

records.change: "the day of Christ" becomes "the day of the Lord"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "the day of the Lord", an Old Testament phrase for God's coming judgment, rather than the distinctly Christian "the day of Christ"; both describe the same coming event.

records.change: "the man of sin" becomes "the man of lawlessness"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "lawlessness" rather than "sin" in this description of the end-times figure; the two words overlap closely in meaning.

records.change: "chosen you from the beginning" becomes "chose you as firstfruits"
records.note: This rests on a one-letter difference in the Greek (ap' arches / aparchen); the earliest manuscripts favour "firstfruits", which emphasises the Thessalonians' early place among the saved rather than God's eternal choice.

records.change: "waiting for Christ" becomes "Christ's perseverance"
records.note: The Greek genitive here is ambiguous; NIV takes it as Christ's own steadfastness, held up as an example, where KJV takes it as the church's patient hope for his return. Both are Pauline themes elsewhere.

records.change: "and Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "and Christ Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Lord" from this second title for Christ our hope; "Lord" is used of him elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: Omits "in Christ" from Paul's oath
records.note: The words "in Christ" after "I speak the truth" are disputed among the manuscripts and left out here; Paul's point, that he is not lying, stands either way.

records.change: "God was manifest" becomes "He appeared"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "who" or "he" rather than "God", likely because the abbreviation for God (ΘΣ) was confused with "who" (ΟΣ) in copying, or the reverse; the deity of Christ, the subject of this hymn, is not otherwise in question.

records.change: "damnation" becomes "judgment"
records.note: The Greek word (krima) means judgment or verdict rather than specifically eternal damnation; this is a translation choice, not a manuscript difference, with NIV closer to the word's ordinary sense and KJV stronger than the context of a broken pledge requires.

records.change: "the Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "Christ Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Lord" from this charge given before God and Christ; the title is used of him elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: Omits "from such withdraw thyself"
records.note: The NIV follows Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and other early witnesses, which lack the command; the Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus have it. Separation from false teachers is still taught in 2 Timothy 3:5.

records.change: "before the Lord" becomes "before God"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "God" rather than "Lord" here; both describe the same solemn witness to right teaching.

records.change: "the name of Christ" becomes "the name of the Lord"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "Lord" rather than "Christ" in this quoted seal; the reference is the same person either way.

records.change: "the Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "Christ Jesus"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts drop "Lord" from this solemn charge given before the judge of the living and the dead; the title is used of him elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: "The Lord Jesus Christ" becomes "The Lord"
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read simply "the Lord" in this closing blessing, without "Jesus Christ"; the fuller title is used throughout the rest of the letter.

records.change: Drops "mercy" and "Lord" from the greeting
records.note: The earliest manuscripts read "grace and peace" rather than "grace, mercy, and peace", and "Christ Jesus our Saviour" rather than "the Lord Jesus Christ our Saviour"; both are shorter forms of Paul's usual greeting.

records.change: Omits "by himself" from purging our sins
records.note: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus lack "by himself"; P46, the Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus have it. Christ's sole work of purification is still stated in Hebrews 9:12-14.

records.change: "I have begotten thee" becomes "I have become your Father"
records.note: Both render the same Greek verb (gennao, to beget) from Psalm 2:7; NIV's wording avoids the word "begotten", long used of the Son's eternal generation from the Father, though the underlying text and meaning are unchanged.

records.change: Omits "and set him over the works of thy hands"
records.note: This clause, from the Greek Old Testament of Psalm 8:6, is missing from the earliest manuscripts of Hebrews and is largely repeated in the next verse; NIV also renders the psalm's "him" as "them", a gender-neutral choice that softens its individual, messianic application to Christ.

records.change: Took on "the nature of angels" becomes "he helps"
records.note: The Greek verb here (epilambanetai) can mean either "takes hold of" or "helps"; NIV's choice describes Christ assisting humanity, where KJV's describes him taking to himself human nature itself, the traditional reading tied to the incarnation.

records.change: "Jesus" becomes "Joshua"
records.note: Both texts translate the same Greek name (Iesous); the NIV supplies the historical referent, Joshua son of Nun, since the passage concerns the conquest generation, not Christ. No doctrine is affected either way.

records.change: "I have begotten thee" becomes "I have become your Father"
records.note: Quoting Psalm 2:7, the Greek verb is literally "I have begotten you"; the NIV renders it relationally rather than literally. The word "begotten" was central to the Arian debate over the Son's eternal generation, and sonship is still affirmed by the surrounding verses.

records.change: Drops "in heaven" describing believers' possessions
records.note: Some early manuscripts (including the first hand of Sinaiticus) lack "in heaven," which the NIV follows, while the Byzantine text behind the KJV retains it. The heavenly, eternal nature of the promised reward is still taught throughout Hebrews (e.g. 11:16).

records.change: Drops "through the Spirit" describing purification
records.note: The phrase "dia pneumatos" appears in the Byzantine text behind the KJV but is absent from the early Alexandrian manuscripts the NIV follows. The Spirit's role in sanctification is stated elsewhere, including two verses earlier (1 Peter 1:2).

records.change: Adds "grow up in your salvation"
records.note: The NIV follows P72, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus, which have "unto salvation"; the Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus lack it. Some read it as salvation being grown into.

records.change: "Sanctify the Lord God" becomes "revere Christ as Lord"
records.note: Manuscripts differ here: the Byzantine text behind the KJV reads "Lord God," the early Alexandrian text behind the NIV reads "Christ as Lord." If anything, the NIV's reading makes the identification of Christ with God more explicit, not less.

records.change: Omits "for us" from Christ's suffering
records.note: Vaticanus and other early witnesses lack "for us"; Sinaiticus' corrector, the Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus have it. Christ's substitutionary suffering is still stated in 1 Peter 2:21 and 3:18.

records.change: Drops "on your part he is glorified"
records.note: The closing clause, "on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified," is missing from the earliest manuscripts and most modern critical editions, though present in the Byzantine text behind the KJV. Its absence doesn't affect the verse's main point about being blessed in suffering for Christ's name.

records.change: "Damnation" becomes "destruction"
records.note: The Greek word (apōleia) is more literally "destruction" or "perdition" than the KJV's strong "damnation." This is a translation choice rather than a manuscript difference, and doesn't by itself settle the question of eternal conscious punishment versus annihilation.

records.change: Drops "for ever" describing reserved darkness
records.note: The words "eis aiōna" (for ever), found in the Byzantine text behind the KJV, are absent from the earlier manuscripts the NIV follows, possibly harmonized in some copies from the parallel wording in Jude 13. Eternal judgment for false teachers is affirmed elsewhere in the same passage.

records.change: "Your joy" becomes "our joy"
records.note: Manuscripts split between hēmōn (our) and hymōn (your); the NIV follows the reading favored in modern critical editions. It affects only whose joy is made complete, not any doctrine.

records.change: "Jesus Christ his Son" becomes "Jesus, his Son"
records.note: Both textual traditions read "Jesus Christ" here; the NIV's dropping of "Christ" is a translation choice, not a manuscript variant. The teaching that the Son's blood cleanses from all sin is unchanged.

records.change: Drops "Christ" and "is come in the flesh"
records.note: A minority of manuscripts read simply "does not confess Jesus," which some modern editions and the NIV follow, against the fuller Byzantine reading behind the KJV, "Jesus Christ is come in the flesh." The fuller confession of the incarnation is made explicitly one verse earlier and elsewhere in the letter.

records.change: "Only begotten Son" becomes "one and only Son"
records.note: The Greek monogenēs is traditionally rendered "only begotten," tied to the doctrine of the Son's eternal generation, but many modern scholars take it to mean "unique" or "one of a kind" rather than describing an act of begetting. Both renderings affirm Christ's unique sonship.

records.change: Drops the Trinitarian formula "Father, Word, Holy Ghost... one"
records.note: This sentence, the "Comma Johanneum," is absent from every early Greek manuscript and first appears in a handful of late medieval copies before entering the Textus Receptus; textual scholars near-universally regard it as a later addition, not part of John's original letter. The Trinity is taught elsewhere in Scripture without depending on this verse.

records.change: The "earthly witnesses" wording loses its added heavenly counterpart
records.note: This verse is the second half of the same interpolation as verse 7 (the "Comma Johanneum"); the NIV's shorter text, "the Spirit, the water and the blood, and the three are in agreement," preserves what is generally regarded as John's actual, single statement, which later copying split into separate heavenly and earthly witnesses.

records.change: Drops the repeated closing clause about believing
records.note: The KJV's final clause, "and that ye may believe on the name of the Son of God," repeats the verse's opening and is missing from the earlier manuscripts the NIV follows, likely an early scribal duplication. Nothing of substance is lost, since the same statement is made earlier in the verse.

records.change: "He keepeth himself" becomes "the One... keeps them safe"
records.note: The Greek "ho gennētheis" (the one born/begotten) is ambiguous: the KJV takes it as the believer keeping himself, the NIV as Christ ("the one born of God") keeping the believer safe. Commentators argue for both readings; this is a translation and interpretive choice, not a manuscript difference.

records.change: Drops "the Lord" before "Jesus Christ"
records.note: Some manuscripts include "kyriou" (Lord) before "Jesus Christ" here and some do not; the NIV follows the shorter reading. Christ's lordship is affirmed throughout the letter regardless of this one title.

records.change: Recasts two Lord titles as naming Christ alone
records.note: The Greek construction ("despotēs kai kyrios") most naturally names one person, Jesus Christ, as both Master and Lord; the KJV's wording can be read as naming two beings, God and Christ, separately. The NIV's rendering, if anything, states Christ's deity more directly.

records.change: Omits "wise"; adds "through Jesus Christ our Lord, before all ages"
records.note: The NIV follows P72, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus; the Byzantine majority and the Textus Receptus lack the added phrases and have "wise". The doxology gains Christ as mediator.

records.change: Omits "the beginning and the ending"; "Lord" becomes "Lord God"
records.note: Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and most Greek manuscripts lack the title and read "Lord God"; the Textus Receptus follows a few late witnesses. The same title stands in Revelation 21:6 and 22:13.

records.change: Drops "Christ" twice from "Jesus Christ"
records.note: Revelation's manuscripts vary considerably on whether "Christ" accompanies "Jesus"; the earlier text the NIV follows lacks it in both places in this verse. Jesus is named plainly either way.

records.change: Drops "I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last"
records.note: This self-declaration is absent from the earliest Greek manuscripts and is thought to have been copied in here from 1:8 and 22:13, where it is undisputed; the NIV omits it accordingly. Christ's identity as Alpha and Omega is stated without dispute elsewhere in Revelation.

records.change: "Hell" becomes "Hades"
records.note: The Greek word is hadēs (the realm of the dead), which the KJV renders "hell" along with the separate word geenna; the NIV keeps the two distinct by transliterating "Hades." Christ's authority over death and the grave is affirmed either way.

records.change: Drops "him that liveth for ever and ever"
records.note: The phrase describing the one worshiped is present in the Byzantine text behind the KJV but missing from earlier manuscripts, likely inserted here from the similar scene in 4:9-10; the NIV follows the shorter text. The eternality of the one worshiped is a repeated theme throughout Revelation regardless.

records.change: "Hell" becomes "Hades"
records.note: As in 1:18, the NIV transliterates hadēs rather than translating it "hell," keeping it distinct from geenna. The personification of Death and Hades as riders is unchanged.

records.change: "An angel" becomes "an eagle"
records.note: Manuscripts genuinely differ here between angelou (angel), behind the KJV, and aetou (eagle), found in some important early witnesses and followed by the NIV. Either way the same three-fold woe is pronounced over the earth.

records.change: "Time no longer" becomes "no more delay"
records.note: The Greek chronos can mean either "time" or "delay"; the KJV's famous rendering suggests the end of time itself, while the NIV (with most modern translations) reads it as the end of the delay before the prophesied events of verse 7. This is a translation choice, not a manuscript difference.

records.change: "The God of the earth" becomes "the Lord of the earth"
records.note: Manuscripts differ between theou (God), behind the KJV, and kyriou (Lord), followed by the NIV. Both titles point to the same divine figure evoking Zechariah 4.

records.change: "The Spirit of life" becomes "the breath of life"
records.note: The Greek pneuma can mean "spirit" or "breath"; the NIV's choice echoes Ezekiel 37's dry bones receiving breath, while the KJV's capitalized "Spirit" suggests the Holy Spirit's direct action. This is a translation choice rather than a textual variant.

records.change: Omits "and art to come"
records.note: The phrase is lacking in nearly all Greek manuscripts, including the Byzantine majority; the Textus Receptus has it from a few late witnesses. Without it the hymn presents God's coming as now fulfilled in his reign; the threefold title stands in 1:4, 1:8 and 4:8.

records.change: "Testimony of Jesus Christ" becomes "testimony about Jesus"
records.note: As elsewhere in Revelation, the NIV's underlying text lacks "Christ" here where the Byzantine text behind the KJV has it. Jesus is still named plainly as the one testified about.

records.change: Drops "before the throne of God"
records.note: The phrase locating their blamelessness "before the throne of God" is present in the Byzantine text behind the KJV but absent from earlier manuscripts the NIV follows. The moral claim that they are blameless remains in both.

records.change: "Holy One" replaces "Lord"; drops "and shalt be"
records.note: The Alexandrian text reads "the Holy One" and drops the future clause, where the Textus Receptus has "Lord ... and shalt be." Both traditions still affirm God's eternal being as "who are and who were."

records.change: Splits "holy apostles" into separate "saints" and "apostles"
records.note: Some early manuscripts add "and" before "apostles," making "saints" a third group rather than an adjective on apostles, as the NIV follows; the Textus Receptus reads "holy apostles and prophets" as one group. Both readings still call the redeemed to rejoice over Babylon's fall.

records.change: Drops "the Lord," keeping only "our God"
records.note: The Alexandrian text omits "Lord" before "our God," which the Textus Receptus retains; both readings still address God directly in the doxology.

records.change: "before God" becomes "before the throne"
records.note: Some early manuscripts read "the throne" for "God" at this judgment scene, a reading the NIV follows; the throne is already established as God's throne in context, so nothing is lost doctrinally.

records.change: "hell" translated as "Hades"
records.note: The NIV transliterates the Greek "Hades" rather than translating it "hell" as the KJV does, keeping the temporary abode of the dead distinct from the final "lake of fire" named two verses later. The judgment described is the same in both versions.

records.change: "hell" translated as "Hades" again
records.note: As in verse 13, the NIV renders the Greek "Hades" instead of "hell," keeping the intermediate state distinct from the "lake of fire" it is cast into here. Both versions describe the same final judgment.

records.change: Voice comes "from the throne," not "out of heaven"
records.note: Some early manuscripts read "the throne" for "heaven" here, a reading the NIV follows; the Textus Receptus's "heaven" and the throne are already the same location in this vision, so nothing doctrinal changes.

records.change: "he shall be my son" becomes "they will be my children"
records.note: The NIV renders the Greek's singular "son" as gender-neutral plural "children," softening the individual sonship language of the text. The status of overcomers as God's own is unchanged either way.

records.change: Drops "of them which are saved" modifying "nations"
records.note: The Textus Receptus specifies that only "the saved" among the nations walk in the city's light, a phrase the Alexandrian text (and NIV) omits. Without it the verse no longer distinguishes saved from unsaved nations, though Revelation 21:27 still excludes the unclean from the city.

records.change: "do his commandments" becomes "wash their robes"
records.note: The Textus Receptus reads "those who do his commandments" while the Alexandrian text reads "those who wash their robes," a well-known variant from similar-sounding Greek words. This shifts the stated basis of the blessing from obedience to cleansing through Christ's blood, though both ideas appear elsewhere in Revelation (7:14; 12:11).

records.change: "book of life" becomes "tree of life"
records.note: Almost all Greek manuscripts read "tree"; "book" entered the Textus Receptus through Erasmus, whose Greek copy lacked these verses and was supplied from the Latin Vulgate. The book of life is still named in 3:5, 20:15 and 21:27.

records.change: Drops "Christ"; "you all" becomes "God's people"
records.note: The Alexandrian text reads "the Lord Jesus" without "Christ," which the Textus Receptus includes, and "his people" instead of "you all." The title of Christ is shortened here, though "Jesus" and "Lord" are both retained.
